title: Doctors
strapline: Take a seat in the waiting room — the doctor will see you now.
intent: Children rehearse a visit that can feel scary in real life — the waiting room, the examination, the injection — until it feels ordinary and manageable.
Caring for a poorly patient stretches empathy: listening to symptoms, being gentle, making someone feel better.
Rich specific vocabulary gets a workout — stethoscope, temperature, bandage, prescription, appointment, X-ray.
The appointment itself is a perfect back-and-forth conversation: 'What seems to be the trouble?' demands a real answer.
Writing has a job to do here — appointment books, prescriptions, patient notes, an eye-test chart on the wall.
Talk about healthy bodies grows naturally: rest, drinks, washing hands, what makes us feel better.
implementation: Take the low-status roles — be the patient with the mysterious tummy ache — so children hold the expert roles of doctor, nurse and receptionist.
Model symptom talk and comfort talk: 'It hurts just here when I breathe in', 'You're being so gentle, thank you doctor.'
Feed in the real words and let children own them: stethoscope, thermometer, plaster, ambulance, prescription.
Set up the whole journey — waiting room chairs, a receptionist's desk with the appointment book, the examination couch — so the play has a structure to travel through.
Draw out body knowledge without lecturing: 'Why do you think I feel so tired? What should I do to get better?'
Leave clipboards, appointment cards and a prescription pad wherever a writer might land.
After a child's real appointment or a period of illness, follow their lead — this is where big feelings about it get processed.
key_questions: What seems to be the trouble today? Where does it hurt?
How will you find out what's wrong with your patient?
What will help this patient feel better — and what should they do at home?
Who's next in the waiting room? How do they know it's their turn?
What do our bodies need every day to stay well?

impact.text: Children re-enact the doctor's visit — checking heartbeats, taking temperatures, giving out plasters — first briefly, then in extended surgery scenes.
Older children run a whole surgery over days — receptionist, doctor, paramedic — with storylines, characters and rules of their own.
Children pick up and correctly use new medical vocabulary: stethoscope, thermometer, prescription, appointment.
Doctor and patient hold a genuine multi-turn consultation — asking about symptoms, listening, replying in role.
Children 'write' prescriptions, patient notes and appointments, and can tell you exactly what each one says.
Children show real tenderness towards their patients — a gentle voice, a careful bandage, a reassuring 'you're going to be fine'.
Children talk about what bodies need to get better and stay well — rest, water, food, warmth — and connect it to their own hungry, thirsty and tired feelings.
Children wrap bandages, fasten slings and handle the doctor's tools with careful, deliberate control.

enhancements: A real appointment book, appointment cards and a bell on the receptionist's desk.
Prescription pads, a rubber stamp and a 'pharmacy' shelf of labelled (empty) medicine boxes.
X-ray images on a light panel or window for children to diagnose broken bones.
An eye-test chart of letters and pictures on the wall.
Bandages, slings, cotton wool and plasters for real wrapping and fastening practice.
A baby clinic day: dolls to be weighed, measured and checked over.
A visit from a real nurse, paramedic or health visitor — then watch the play grow.

playing_exploring: Children replay real and sometimes worrying experiences at their own pace, in charge for once.
Every prop begs to be tested — what does the stethoscope actually let me hear?
active_learning: The patient must be made better: children stay with a self-chosen goal through examination, diagnosis and cure.
creating_thinking: Children link cause and effect — she's hot, so she needs medicine and rest — and invent their own treatments and storylines.
